{{Short description|Mathematical series}}
A '''Neumann series''' is a [[series (mathematics)|mathematical series]] that sums ''k''-times repeated applications of an [[Operator (physics)|operator]] <math>T </math>. This has the generator form
:<math> \sum_{k=0}^\infty T^k </math>
where <math>T^k </math> is the ''k''-times repeated application of <math>T </math>; <math>T^0 </math> is the [[identity operator]] <math>I </math> and <math>T^k := {}T^{k-1}\circ{T}</math> for <math>k > 0 </math>. This is a special case of the generalization of a [[geometric series]] of real or complex numbers to a geometric series of operators. The generalized initial term of the series is the identity operator <math>T^0 = I</math> and the generalized common ratio of the series is the operator <math>T.</math>

The series is named after the mathematician [[Carl Neumann]], who used it in 1877 in the context of [[potential theory]]. The Neumann series is used in [[functional analysis]]. It is closely connected to the [[resolvent formalism]] for studying the [[spectrum (functional analysis)|spectrum]] of bounded operators and, applied from the left to a function, it forms the [[Liouville-Neumann series]] that formally solves [[Fredholm integral equation]]s.

== Properties ==

Suppose that <math>T</math> is a bounded linear operator on the [[normed vector space]] <math>X</math>. If the Neumann series [[Convergent series|converges]] in the [[operator norm]], then <math>I-T</math> is [[Invertible matrix|invertible]] and its inverse is the series:
:<math> (I - T)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty T^k </math>,
where <math> I </math> is the [[identity operator]] in <math>X</math>.  To see why, consider the partial sums
:<math>S_n := \sum_{k=0}^n T^k</math>.
Then we have
:<math>\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}(I-T)S_n = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(\sum_{k=0}^n T^k - \sum_{k=0}^n T^{k+1}\right) = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(I - T^{n+1}\right) = I</math>
This result on operators is analogous to [[geometric series]] in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.

One case in which convergence is guaranteed is when <math>X</math> is a [[Banach space]] and <math>|T| <1</math> in the operator norm; another compatible case is that <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^\infty |T^k|</math> converges. However, there are also results which give weaker conditions under which the series converges.

== Example == 
Let <math>C\in \R^{3 \times 3}</math> be given by:
:<math>
\begin{pmatrix}
0  & \frac{1}{2}  & \frac{1}{4} \\
\frac{5}{7} & 0 & \frac{1}{7} \\
\frac{3}{10} & \frac{3}{5} & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
For the Neumann series <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^n C^k</math> to converge to <math>(I-C)^{-1}</math>  as <math>n</math> goes to infinity, the [[Matrix_norm#Spectral_norm_(p_=_2)|spectral norm]] of <math>C</math> must be smaller than unity. This norm is about <math>0.9056</math> as can be checked numerically (e.g., by computing the singular values),
confirming that the Neumann series converges.

== Approximate matrix inversion ==
A truncated Neumann series can be used for [[Invertible_matrix#By_Neumann_series|approximate matrix inversion]]. To approximate the inverse of an invertible matrix <math>A</math>, consider that

<math>\begin{align}
A^{-1} &= (I - I + A)^{-1} \\
& = (I - (I - A))^{-1} \\
& = (I - T)^{-1}
\end{align}</math>

for <math>T =(I - A).</math> Then, using the Neumann series identity that <math display="inline">\sum_{k=0}^\infty T^k = (I - T)^{-1}</math> if the appropriate norm condition on <math>T = (I - A)</math> is satisfied, <math display="inline">A^{-1} = (I - (I - A))^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (I - A)^k.</math> Since these terms shrink with increasing <math>k,</math> given the conditions on the norm, then truncating the series at some finite <math>n</math> may give a practical approximation to the inverse matrix:
:<math>A^{-1} \approx \sum_{k=0}^n (I- A)^k.</math>

== The set of invertible operators is open ==
A corollary is that the set of invertible operators between two Banach spaces <math> B </math> and <math> B' </math> is open in the topology induced by the operator norm. Indeed, let <math> S : B \to B' </math> be an invertible operator and let <math> T: B \to B' </math> be another operator. 
If <math>|S-T| < |S^{-1}|^{-1} </math>, then <math>T</math> is also invertible. 
Since <math> |I - S^{-1}T| < 1 </math>, the Neumann series <math display="inline"> \sum_{k=0}^\infty (I-S^{-1}T)^k </math> is convergent. Therefore, we have
:<math> T^{-1}S = (I - (I - S^{-1}T))^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty(I - S^{-1}T)^k </math>

Taking the norms, we get
:<math> |T^{-1}S| \le \frac{1}{1 - | I - (S^{-1}T)|} </math>

The norm of <math> T^{-1} </math> can be bounded by
:<math> |T^{-1}| \le \tfrac{1}{1-q} |S^{-1}| \quad\text{where}\quad q = |S-T| \, |S^{-1}|. </math>

== Applications ==
The Neumann series has been used for linear data detection in massive multiuser [[multiple-input multiple-output]] (MIMO) wireless systems. Using a truncated Neumann series avoids computation of an explicit matrix inverse, which reduces the complexity of linear data detection from cubic to square.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Wu|first1=M.|last2=Yin|first2=B.|last3=Vosoughi|first3=A.|last4=Studer|first4=C.|last5=Cavallaro|first5=J. R.|last6=Dick|first6=C.|title=2013 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS2013) |chapter=Approximate matrix inversion for high-throughput data detection in the large-scale MIMO uplink |date=May 2013|pages=2155–2158|doi=10.1109/ISCAS.2013.6572301|hdl=1911/75011|isbn=978-1-4673-5762-3 |s2cid=389966 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Another application is the theory of [[propagation graph|propagation graphs]] which takes advantage of Neumann series to derive closed form expressions for transfer functions.
